newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU pledges to clamp down on 'subsidy shopping'.
newsitem.headline: EU pledges to clamp down on 'subsidy shopping'.

text.p: The European Commission said on Friday it was exploring ways of clamping down on a growing trend to relocate business operations in the European Union to take advantage of national and EU subsidies.

"(European Competiton Commissioner Karel) Van Miert will submit a document to the Commission in the following weeks to find out how we can use competition rules to prevent companies from doing what is commonly called 'aid shopping'," Van Miert's spokesman told a news briefing.
The announcement follows the surprise decision by Renault to close a Belgian assembly plant in Vilvoorde and increase production at its northern Spanish subsidiary in Valladolid.

But the spokesman said the Commission's discussions would have no influence on the controversial Renault move. This was because the Commission's competition services were only looking into the possibility that some companies were playing off poor European regions which benefit from EU development funds and favourable rules on government subsidies against each other.
Vilvoorde, situated north of Brussels, is not eligible for EU funds. Vallodolid is in the province of Castille-Leon, one of the EU's less developed areas.

Renault's decision to close its profitable Belgian plant with the loss of 3,100 jobs came only a few days before Spain asked the Commission to clear 11 million European currency units ($12.4 million) in aid to help the French carmaker increase production in Valladolid.

The request provoked an angry reaction from Van Miert on Thursday who said he would block the subsidies until Renault changed its attitude. Renault is being accused of flouting Belgian and EU rules on informing and consulting staff on key strategic decisions.
The huge row surrounding the affair has caused the Spanish government to suspend the aid request, although the official reason was said to be a "technical" one.

It became clear on Friday that not only Spanish funds are involved as the Commission said at first. Seven million Ecus would be financed by the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF), the spokeswoman for Regional Policy Commissioner Monika Wulf-Mathies told reporters.
"We get evidence every day that national authorities cheat; yesterday they had not told us that the ERDF was involved," a Commission official said, commenting on the Spanish request.
Wulf-Mathies's spokeswoman said the Commission would also carry out a thorough reform of its structural funds policy before 1999 to avoid relocation moves.

"We want to promote regional development...but pure profiting from aid needs to be ruled out," the official said speaking on the condition of anonymity. This could be done by making aid conditional on long-term investment. ($1 = 0.883 Ecus)
